heading: VPN
subtitle: A WireGuard VPN to an exit run by TNP. Use it on your router, so every device at home is covered, or on a phone or computer with the official WireGuard app. Keys are made in this browser; TNP only ever receives the public key.
loadError: Your VPN devices could not be loaded.

unavailable.heading: Not available yet
unavailable.body: TNP has not switched on its first exit yet, so devices cannot be added. This page will let you add them as soon as it does. Nothing has been stored for your account.

notAllowed.heading: Not available for your account
notAllowed.body: The VPN is open to a limited group of accounts for now, while TNP keeps the exits' capacity and cost fixed, and yours is not in it yet. Nothing has been stored for your account. No exit accepts devices added earlier while your account is not in the group.

honesty.heading: What this VPN protects, and what it does not
honesty.protects1: From your local network (public Wi-Fi, other people on your router) and your internet provider: they see an encrypted WireGuard connection to a TNP exit, not the sites you visit, your DNS lookups or what you send.
honesty.protects2: Your IP address from the sites you visit: they see the exit's address instead.
honesty.not1: From TNP. Oxy operates the exit, so it can technically see which addresses and ports you connect to, and the content of anything the site itself does not encrypt. HTTPS hides the content, not which site you reach. Exits keep only totals, never per-connection records, but you are trusting us on that.
honesty.not2: Your identity. This is not anonymity: one company runs the exit and knows which account each device belongs to, and someone able to watch both your connection and the exit can match them by timing.
honesty.not3: What you tell a site. Signing in to an account identifies you, VPN or not.
honesty.not4: From the hosting provider (AWS), which can observe the exit's traffic like any network operator.
honesty.tor: If your safety depends on not being identified, for example as an activist or journalist facing a government, use <link>Tor Browser</link> instead of this VPN. TNP's private, multi-hop tier does not exist yet.
honesty.stored: What TNP stores for each device: the name you give it, its public key and its tunnel address. Never its private key, never when it connects, from which IP address, or how much it sends.
honesty.ipv6: IPv6 is not carried yet. The tunnel captures it so it cannot leak around the VPN, and the exit refuses it, so your apps use IPv4.

add.heading: Add a device
add.intro: Give the device a name you will recognise. A WireGuard key pair is generated in this browser; only the public key is sent to TNP.
add.name: Device name
add.limit: You have {{max}} devices, the most an account can have. Revoke one to add another.
add.failed: The device could not be added.

config.heading: Set up {{name}}
config.once: This is the only time the private key is shown. TNP never received it and cannot show it again. Download the configuration or scan the code now; if you lose it, revoke the device and add a new one.
config.clipboard: Copying puts the private key in your clipboard, where clipboard history or sync can keep it. Prefer the download or the QR code. If you do copy, this page overwrites the clipboard after 60 seconds where the browser allows it.
config.exitHelp: Choose the exit nearest you: it is faster, and websites answer from servers near it. This device is accepted at every exit, but each configuration names one, so to switch exits, choose another here and download or scan its configuration too.
config.dnsOnExit: DNS: {{dns}}, the TNP resolver on the exit itself, reached through the tunnel. It answers from near the exit and keeps no record of the names you look up.
config.dnsVia: DNS: {{dns}}, the TNP resolver, reached through the tunnel. It keeps no record of the names you look up.
config.qrLabel: WireGuard configuration for {{name}} as a QR code
config.qrHelp: The code contains the private key. Do not photograph it or share your screen while it is visible.

phone.step1: Install the official WireGuard app, published by WireGuard Development Team, from Google Play, F-Droid or the App Store.
phone.step2: Tap +, choose Scan from QR code and scan the code above. Name the tunnel, for example tnp.
phone.android: Android kill switch: Settings, Network, VPN, the gear next to WireGuard, then turn on Always-on VPN and Block connections without VPN.
phone.ios: iOS: in the tunnel's settings, turn on On-Demand activation so it reconnects by itself.

desktop.step1: Install WireGuard from wireguard.com/install (on macOS, from the Mac App Store).
desktop.step2: Download the configuration above, then choose Import tunnel(s) from file and select it.
desktop.windows: On Windows, a full tunnel like this one blocks all traffic outside the tunnel while it is active, so nothing leaks if the connection drops.

linux.intro: Download the configuration, then, in the folder you saved it to:
linux.boot: To start it at every boot: sudo systemctl enable --now wg-quick@{{name}}
linux.dns: wg-quick sets DNS through resolvconf or systemd-resolved. If neither is installed, your DNS does not change and lookups bypass the tunnel's resolver.

openwrt.intro: WireGuard is built into OpenWrt. Set it up once on the router and every device on your network uses the VPN without installing anything.
openwrt.packages: Install the packages once: System, Software, or over SSH opkg update && opkg install luci-proto-wireguard (OpenWrt 25 and later: apk add luci-proto-wireguard), then reboot the router.
openwrt.luci1: Network, Interfaces, Add new interface: name wg0, protocol WireGuard VPN.
openwrt.luci2: General Settings: click Load configuration… and paste the router configuration below (OpenWrt 23.05 and later). It dials the exit by IP address, because the router cannot look up a name before its tunnel is up. On older versions, paste the private key and add the address {{ipv4}}/32 by hand.
openwrt.luci3: Peers: check that the TNP exit peer has Route Allowed IPs ticked and Persistent Keep Alive set to 25.
openwrt.luci4: Advanced Settings: Use custom DNS servers, {{dns}}. Then edit the wan interface and untick Use DNS servers advertised by peer, so lookups do not go to your provider.
openwrt.luci5: Firewall Settings: create a new zone named tnp. In Network, Firewall, set zone tnp to input reject, forward reject, with Masquerading and MSS clamping on, and allow zone lan to forward to tnp.
openwrt.luci6: IPv6: edit the wan6 interface and, under Advanced Settings, untick IPv6 source routing. Then in Network, Firewall, Traffic Rules, add a rule for IPv6 from zone lan to zones wan and tnp with action reject. Without this, devices on your network send IPv6 straight to your provider, outside the tunnel.
openwrt.luci7: Kill switch: in Network, Firewall, edit zone lan and untick wan under Allow forward to destination zones, so devices have no internet rather than using your provider when the tunnel is down.
openwrt.luci8: Save & Apply. Status, WireGuard should show a recent handshake within a minute.
openwrt.routerConfigHeading: Router configuration (dials the exit by IP address)
openwrt.cliHeading: Or over SSH, all at once
openwrt.cliNote: These commands contain this device's private key. Paste them into the router's shell and do not save them anywhere else. The connection may drop for a few seconds while the network restarts.
openwrt.killText: These commands remove the forwarding from your LAN to your provider: if the tunnel is down, devices on your network have no internet instead of silently using your provider. The router itself keeps using wan, because it needs it to reach the exit.
openwrt.killToggle: Keep a fallback to my provider when the tunnel is down (not recommended: traffic then leaves without the VPN, and you will not notice)
openwrt.ipv6: IPv6 is not carried yet. The commands switch off IPv6 source routing and make the router refuse IPv6 from your LAN with an immediate error, so none of it leaves outside the tunnel. To stop devices trying IPv6 at all, also turn off router advertisements on the LAN (Network, Interfaces, lan, DHCP Server, IPv6 Settings).
openwrt.fallbackText: To let devices use your provider again when the tunnel is down:
openwrt.removeText: Deletes the tunnel and firewall rules, and restores your provider's DNS, IPv6 source routing and forwarding:

devices.heading: Your devices
devices.lost: Lost a phone or a config? Revoke the device. Exits stop accepting its key at their next sync, normally within a minute; an exit that cannot reach TNP stops accepting every device after 10 minutes.
devices.failed: That did not work. Try again.
devices.revokeConfirm: Revoke {{name}}? Exits stop accepting it at their next sync (normally within a minute, at most about 10 minutes) and its configuration cannot be used again.
